title: Frozen yogurt
wiki_lead:
Frozen yogurt is a frozen dessert, usually made with yogurt as its primary ingredient. Frozen yogurt is similar in composition to ice cream, with its main ingredient being milk or milk substitute.
Frozen yogurt for retail sale is typically manufactured from a mixture of milk ingredients, sweeteners, stabilizers, and yogurt cultures. After fermentation, the mixture is cooled, aged, flavored, and frozen while air is introduced to improve texture and flavor. The product may be distributed as soft serve, or hardened for serving by the scoop. It is commonly eaten with toppings such as candy pieces, fruit, nuts, chocolate, or syrup.
Branded frozen yogurt products were marketed in the United States from the late 1960s and 1970s. They became widely popular in the United States in the 1980s as a lower-fat alternative to ice cream, declined during the 1990s, and had a resurgence around 2005-2014 involving tart flavors and self-serve shops.
wiki_fulltext:
Frozen yogurt is a frozen dessert, usually made with yogurt as its primary ingredient. Frozen yogurt is similar in composition to ice cream, with its main ingredient being milk or milk substitute.
Frozen yogurt for retail sale is typically manufactured from a mixture of milk ingredients, sweeteners, stabilizers, and yogurt cultures. After fermentation, the mixture is cooled, aged, flavored, and frozen while air is introduced to improve texture and flavor. The product may be distributed as soft serve, or hardened for serving by the scoop. It is commonly eaten with toppings such as candy pieces, fruit, nuts, chocolate, or syrup.
Branded frozen yogurt products were marketed in the United States from the late 1960s and 1970s. They became widely popular in the United States in the 1980s as a lower-fat alternative to ice cream, declined during the 1990s, and had a resurgence around 2005-2014 involving tart flavors and self-serve shops.  


Description
The Encyclopedia of Food Sciences and Nutrition defines frozen yogurt as:

A fermented milk or yogurt mix containing a typical yogurt flavor and has been subjected to fermentation by the two yogurt bacteria to a pH of 4.5 or lower or a titratible acidity of 0.9% or higher, expressed as lactic acid.
As of 2013, most countries do not have regulatory standards for frozen yogurt. In the United States, the term frozen yogurt is not strictly defined by a federal standard of identity unlike yogurt or ice cream, but standards for frozen yogurt exist in at least 15 U.S. states as of 2013. Many frozen yogurt products sold in the United States are primarily ice cream blended with a small amount of yogurt.

The government of the Netherlands defines frozen yogurt as having at least 70% yogurt content with a pH of 5.0 or lower, while the government of Australia defines it as having at least 45% yogurt content with a pH of 4.5 or lower.  


Types and presentation

Frozen yogurt is produced in a variety of flavors. Some types of frozen yogurt are more tart in taste, whereas other variations may be sweeter and more similar in taste to ice cream. 
Frozen yogurt is typically eaten from bowls or cups. Frozen yogurt can also be served as a cone, a sandwich or a bar, and is sometimes artistically molded, for example to resemble fruit. It is sometimes substituted for ice cream in frozen blended drinks.


Dietary restrictions
Some frozen yogurt is vegan. Dairy-free frozen yogurt is produced using a plant-based beverage, or plant milk, such as coconut, almond, oat, or soy milk, as its primary base. Frozen yogurt is also sold in halal and kosher varieties.


History


Early history

Frozen yogurt was available in the United States by 1951, when a piece in the Idaho Statesman reported that "there's even a place for health fans in the ice cream world. Most popular is the frozen yogurt that comes in many delicious flavors." Yogurt had reached the US in the late 19th century, but only came to the attention of the broader US market in the 1920s, 1930s and 1940s, through the work of firms like Colombo Yogurt and Gaymont Laboratories Inc. of Stephen A. Gaymont. By August 1969, Gaymont Laboratories was selling a frozen yogurt product under the name "Yogo", with plans to sell it nationally. Upon Gaymont's death, several obituaries credited Yogo as the first frozen yogurt, and Gaymont as its creator.


1960s–1970s
Several sources propose that frozen yogurt was invented in the United States during the latter half of the 1960s or early 1970s. In one account, the Bloomingdale's department store commissioned Massachusetts dairy producer HP Hood to develop a low-fat alternative to ice cream in the early 1970s. The resulting product, marketed as Frogurt, was served at Bloomingdale's Forty Carrots restaurant in New York City by 1972. Companies such as Danone and Häagen-Dazs were selling frozen yogurt in shops by 1976, often offering added toppings or mix-ins.  HP Hood began distributing the product throughout the United States in 1977. In the Chicago area, frozen yogurt was already available in 1977 in supermarkets, restaurants, and storefront shops. In 1978, Boston-based ice cream shop Brigham's Ice Cream created a packaged frozen yogurt, called Humphreez Yogart. The term "Fro-Yo" emerged in this era.


1980s–1990s
Demand for frozen yogurt in the United States expanded during the 1980s, as consumers sought out health foods and low-fat alternatives to ice cream. Between 1985 and 1989, sales in the US grew sixfold to US$1.2 billion, and by the following year frozen yogurt accounted for 14% of all frozen dessert sales. Market research credited chains with much of this growth: McDonald's replaced ice cream with frozen yogurt, and ice cream chains such as Dairy Queen and Baskin-Robbins added it to their menus. In chains such as TCBY and Tasti D-Lite, sweetened frozen yogurt resembling soft serve became available. In The New York Times, the frozen yogurt of the end of the decade was reportedly much less tart than it was earlier, as manufacturers reduced the yogurt content, and quoted a food scientist as saying "frozen yogurt has lost its yogurt".
Frozen yogurt was not regulated by any specific guidelines during the period. In 1991, the FDA proposed establishing a federal standard of identity for frozen yogurt but the agency formally withdrew the proposed rule due to a lack of industry consensus and shifting priorities.[1] Most frozen yogurt of the time contained between 0 and 4% fat. Consumption continued to grow into the 1990s. Consumption per capita in America increased from 1.2 pounds (0.54 kg) in 1987 to 4.4 pounds (2.0 kg) in 1992, as ice cream consumption dipped. Peak sales came in 1994, reaching US$1.7 billion, and subsequently contracted; in figures from the International Dairy Foods Association, annual US production in 2005 had almost halved from the approximately 117 million US gallons (440 ML) made in 1990. Industry analysts later described the first boom as one in which mall-based chains multiplied, competed for the same customers, and then collapsed.


2000s–2010s

Tart frozen yogurt experienced a comeback throughout the 2000s. An early store specializing in tart frozen yogurt during the decade was Pinkberry, started in 2005 in West Hollywood, California. After a 2007 lawsuit accused Pinkberry's products of failing to meet California's standards for frozen yogurt, Pinkberry dropped all yogurt branding until 2008, when the lawsuit was settled and Pinkberry officially became "frozen yogurt". Red Mango entered the U.S. market in 2006. Pinkberry opened two more locations in its second year and attracted venture capital, including a US$27.5 million investment from a fund started by Howard Schultz.
The increasing ubiquity of tart frozen yogurt chain shops led to an expansion in the number of self-service frozen yogurt shops. In 2008, the New York City shop 16 Handles was one of the earliest stores to provide sweeter varieties, which were preferred over the previous flavors. The growing availability of sweeter varieties overall contributed to a shift away from the tart flavors of the mid-2000s. The format was easy to copy, requiring little more than a storefront and a few soft-serve machines; many shops let customers serve themselves and charged by the ounce. Franchising, suppliers of frozen yogurt mix, and would-be owners seeking small businesses after the Great Recession drove rapid expansion, especially between 2011 and 2014.
The expansion of the frozen yogurt industry was supported by the investment of private equity in chains and the growth of franchising. According to market research firm IBISWorld, the number of frozen yogurt shops in the United States increased from an estimated 983 in 2007 to approximately 1,227 in 2016. IBISWorld estimated that the industry would generate approximately US$800 million in revenue in 2013. During this period, private equity firms invested in chains including TCBY, Red Mango, and Sweet Frog.
In 2013, the frozen yogurt market was described by the Wall Street Journal as an oversaturated "retail kudzu" due to the rapid proliferation of identical businesses. By 2014, growth in the frozen yogurt industry had begun to slow amid increasing competition and concerns about market saturation. Some chains diversified their offerings, introducing products such as juices and other desserts. Pinkberry peaked at 154 locations in 2014 and had 71 by the end of 2021, while several other chains fell by 60% or more from their peaks, mostly through closures. According to market research firm Circana, the number of American frozen yogurt stores declined 35% from 2017 to 2024.


2020s–present
Frozen yogurt became popular again in the mid-2020s, a period that journalist Rachel Kurzius called a "third wave". Earlier booms had emphasized what frozen yogurt lacked, such as fat and calories; marketing in the 2020s instead stressed protein, live cultures and other added ingredients, and some brands used Greek yogurt or kefir. Writers also linked the trend to nostalgia and social media.
In the United States, the number of frozen yogurt servings sold between March 2025 and March 2026 increased by 26% compared with the preceding year, according to Circana. Sales of pre-packaged frozen yogurt also increased by 24% over the same period, according to NIQ. Journalists writing about queues at New York City frozen yogurt stores noted that people standing in line often socialized with each other, and connected the trend to the decline of third places in the United States.


Nutritional content

The nutritional value of frozen yogurt can vary, as the added sugar, serving size, protein content, and ingredients may differ, with some brands containing higher amounts of added sugar or saturated fat. The addition of toppings, such as fresh fruit, candies, and sauces, also increases the caloric total. Because formulations differ, products that appear similar can vary considerably in sugar and fat content. Reporting since the 1970s has described frozen yogurt as lower in fat than ice cream, though some products have nearly as many calories.
While frozen yogurt may contain live and active bacterial cultures, it generally contains fewer active cultures than regular yogurt. This is because commercial freezing processes place the microorganisms into a dormant state, and some bacteria lose viability during prolonged cold storage. The survival of these cultures depends on the bacterial strains, manufacturing methods, storage temperature, and how long the product is stored. Some products sold as frozen yogurt do not contain live cultures due to the yogurt base being heat-treated, which kills the cultures. Other manufacturers use yogurt powder to recreate the tart flavor without adding bacterial cultures.
Probiotic organisms, such as Bifidobacterium and L. acidophilus, can be added to frozen yogurt if the pH is around or below 4.0–4.5.


Production

Frozen yogurt consists of milk solids, a sweetener, milk fat, yogurt culture (commonly L. bulgaricus and S. thermophilus), plus flavorings and sometimes coloring (natural or artificial). The base ingredient in frozen yogurt is pasteurized milk, which is cooled before bacterial cultures are introduced. Stabilizers and emulsifiers are added in small amounts to obtain the characteristic whipped texture.
Milk fat accounts for around 0.5–6% of the frozen yogurt. It adds richness and enhances flavor. Milk solids-not-fat (MSNF), consisting of 55% milk sugar (lactose), 37% protein (to reduce melting and add smoothness), and 8% minerals, account for 8–14% of the total volume. MSNF solids are balanced inversely with the milk fat to achieve the desired texture. According to the International Frozen Yogurt Association, the most common sweeteners used for frozen yogurt are sucrose, high-fructose corn syrup (or normal corn syrup), fructose, stevia, sucralose, and aspartame.

grok_lead: Frozen yogurt, commonly known as froyo, is a semi-frozen dessert made by freezing a pasteurized mixture of dairy ingredients, sweeteners, and live bacterial cultures such as Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus, resulting in a creamy texture and tangy flavor that blends elements of ice cream and yogurt. It typically contains at least 3.25% milkfat by weight and 8.25% milk solids not fat, with a titratable acidity of at least 0.3% lactic acid to ensure fermentation has occurred. Unlike traditional ice cream and refrigerated yogurt (the latter standardized at a finished-product pH of 4.6 or lower), frozen yogurt is not defined by a federal standard of identity from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Certain states fill the gap with composition and labeling rules that confirm fermentation and, in some jurisdictions, forbid heat or other bacteriostatic treatment after culturing that would destroy the organisms. It originated as a lower-calorie alternative to ice cream in the United States during the 1970s and gained popularity in the 1980s amid health trends.
